questions.a: A puddle in the yard shrinks as the hot sun shines on it
o: A puddle in the yard shrinks as the hot sun shines on it
The leaves of the neem tree rustle and the branches sway
Uniforms on the clothes line in the hostel swing to and fro
The pages of an open register flutter when the fan is on

questions.q: A label on a jar in the science lab reads 'Air: 21% oxygen'. Lata reasons, 'So the other 79% of the air in the jar must all be nitrogen.' Which correction is right?
questions.a: Nitrogen is 78%; the last 1% is argon, carbon dioxide and other gases
o: Nitrogen is 78%; the last 1% is argon, carbon dioxide and other gases
Nitrogen is 79%, because argon and carbon dioxide are not found in air
Nitrogen is only 21%, the same share as the oxygen in the jar
The other 79% is mostly carbon dioxide, with a little nitrogen in it

questions.q:
Read the statements about air.
Statement 1: Nitrogen and oxygen together make up exactly 100% of the air around the Earth.
Statement 2: We can survive without food or water for a few days, but not without oxygen for even a few minutes.
Statement 3: A gentle breeze and a storm are both wind; they differ in how fast the air moves.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: Kabir holds his paper firki still in a closed room with the fan switched off, and it does not turn. Then he runs across the playground holding it, and it spins fast. What best explains the difference?
questions.a: Running makes air move past the blades, and moving air (wind) turns the firki
o: Running makes air move past the blades, and moving air (wind) turns the firki
Running adds extra oxygen to the blades, and oxygen is what turns the firki
Air is present only outdoors, so the firki can turn only on the playground
Sunlight on the playground heats the paper blades, and that heat turns the firki

questions.q: In one deep breath Bhoomi takes about 500 mL of air into her lungs. Of this, about ___ mL is the gas without which she cannot survive for even a few minutes. (Write the number only.)

questions.a: Drying red chillies spread out on the roof

Grinding wheat in the windmill's flour mill
Pulling water up from the well with the windmill
Winnowing chaff from the wheat by tossing it in the breeze

questions.q:

questions.q: Neha can hold her breath for 40 seconds. She says, 'If I practise every day, one day I will stay underwater for an hour without breathing.' Which fact from the chapter shows why this cannot happen?
questions.a: We cannot survive without oxygen for even a few minutes
o: We cannot survive without oxygen for even a few minutes
We cannot survive without water for even a few minutes
Holding the breath fills the lungs with too much nitrogen
Air in the lungs turns into wind if it is held too long

questions.q: Surya wants his paper firki to spin faster without touching its blades. Which of these will work?
questions.a: Holding it in front of a table fan switched to a higher speed
o: Holding it in front of a table fan switched to a higher speed
Holding it still in bright sunshine so the paper warms up
Keeping it inside a closed cupboard where the air is still
Breathing in deeply while holding it close to his mouth

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column I with the idea about air it shows in Column II.
Column I | Column II
1. Pages of a book flutter when the fan is switched on | a. Wind's energy used to generate electricity
2. Rows of windmills on a windy hilltop | b. The body is short of oxygen
3. Holding your breath soon feels uncomfortable | c. Nitrogen's share of air
4. 78 blue squares in a grid of 100 squares | d. Air is present, and it is moving
True or False? 'On a still night with the fan off, nothing in a closed room rustles or flutters, so there is no air in the room.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Rustling leaves or fluttering pages show only moving air, which is wind. Air, a mixture of gases (nitrogen, oxygen and others), is still present in the room: the people sleeping there keep breathing in its oxygen, without which they could not survive even a few minutes.
s: Verdict: False
Rustling shows only moving air (wind); still air is still there, as breathing its oxygen shows

questions.q:
Kabir holds his firki in front of a table fan. At speed 1 it turns slowly; at speed 5 it whirls.
(a) Which speed is more like a breeze and which more like a storm?
(b) Using (a), explain why a windmill flour mill stops altogether on a day with no wind.
questions.a: (a) Speed 1 is like a breeze (air moving gently); speed 5 is like a storm (air moving fast). (b) The wings of a windmill, like the firki, are turned only by moving air; with no wind there is no moving air, so the wings do not turn and the mill stops.
s: Part (a): speed 1 a breeze, speed 5 a storm, by how fast the air moves
Part (b): only moving air turns the wings, so no wind means no grinding

questions.q:
Bhoomi says, 'My firki and the windmill near the highway work in the same way.'
(a) What makes both of them turn?
(b) Give two useful jobs a windmill can do that a firki cannot.
questions.a: (a) Wind, that is, moving air, rotates the blades of the firki and the wings of the windmill. (b) Any two: running a flour mill, pulling up water from a well, generating electricity.
s: Part (a): wind (moving air) turns both
Part (b): two windmill jobs from flour mill, pulling water from a well, generating electricity

questions.q: Kabir says, 'Air and wind are just two names for the same thing.' Give one way in which he is right and one way in which he is wrong, with an example for the second.
questions.a: Right: wind is air; it is made of the same mixture of gases. Wrong: wind is air that is moving; the still air in a closed room is air but not wind, while the air that sways clothes on a line is wind.
s: Same: wind is air, the same mixture of gases
Different: wind is moving air, with an example of still air versus moving air

questions.q:
A company plans a windmill farm, an area with a large number of windmills.
(a) What do the windmills of such a farm produce?
(b) Why would the company choose an open, windy hilltop rather than a sheltered valley where the air is often still?
questions.a: (a) Electricity, using the energy of the wind. (b) Windmill wings turn only when moving air pushes them; on a windy hilltop they turn for more of the time, so more electricity is made than in a valley where the air is often still.
s: Part (a): electricity from the energy of the wind
Part (b): wings turn only in moving air, so a windy site keeps them turning longer

questions.q: Pranav writes in his notebook: 'Air is a mixture of gases. It is mostly oxygen, and that is why we cannot survive without it.' Check his claim and correct it where needed.
questions.a: Partly right. Air is indeed a mixture of gases, and we need its oxygen for survival. But air is not mostly oxygen: nitrogen makes up 78% and oxygen only 21%.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right parts: air is a mixture, and oxygen is needed for survival
Wrong part corrected: nitrogen 78%, oxygen 21%, so air is mostly nitrogen

questions.q: A picture shows three scenes. Scene 1: a paper firki held still in a closed room with the fan switched off. Scene 2: the same firki held in front of a fan that is switched on. Scene 3: a windmill on a hill on a calm day, its flag hanging straight down. For each scene, say whether the blades turn and give the reason.
questions.a: Scene 1: the blades do not turn, because the air in the closed room is still; there is no wind. Scene 2: the blades turn, because the fan makes the air move and moving air (wind) turns the firki. Scene 3: the wings do not turn; the flag hanging straight down shows the air is calm, so there is no wind to turn them.
s: Scene 1: no turning, the air is still
Scene 2: turns, the fan makes wind
Scene 3: no turning, the limp flag shows there is no wind

questions.q: The answer to a question is: 'Because the wind dropped.' Write a question about a firki, a windmill or a kite for which this is the correct answer, and explain, using the chapter, why the answer fits.
questions.a: E.g. 'The village flour mill ground wheat all morning, but at noon its wings stopped. Why?' Windmill wings are turned by wind, that is, moving air; when the wind dropped, there was no moving air to turn the wings, so the mill stopped grinding.
s: A question about a firki, windmill or kite that stops turning or falls
Wind is moving air that turns the blades or wings
Link: when the wind drops, nothing turns them

questions.q:
A village on a windy hillside in Gujarat grinds its wheat in a windmill flour mill. When the wind is strong enough the mill grinds 40 kg of wheat an hour; on calm days its wings do not turn. Last week the wind was strong enough on 5 days, for 6 hours each day. The village needs about 900 kg of flour a week.
(a) How much wheat was ground last week, and how much more than the need is that?
(b) Work backwards: how many hours of strong wind does the village need in a week to meet its need? How many 6-hour windy days is that, at the least?
(c) Using the chapter, explain why the mill can grind nothing on a calm day.
(d) The panchayat wants to store the extra flour from windy weeks instead of buying an electric mill. Is that a sound plan? Give a judgement that uses your answers.
questions.a: (a) 5 x 6 x 40 = 1,200 kg; 1,200 - 900 = 300 kg more than needed. (b) 900 / 40 = 22.5 hours; 22.5 / 6 = 3.75, so at least 4 windy days of 6 hours. (c) The wings are turned only by wind, that is, moving air; on a calm day the air does not move, so the wings stay still. (d) A judgement such as: storing works for a week with 4 or more windy days, and one good week leaves 300 kg spare, but a fully calm week needs 900 kg from the store, three good weeks' surplus, so storing alone is risky; an electric mill as backup avoids that, at a cost. Credit either view if it uses these figures.
s: Part (a): 1,200 kg, 300 kg extra
Part (b): 22.5 hours, at least 4 windy days
Part (c): only moving air turns the wings
Part (d): a judgement on storing that uses the 300 kg surplus and the calm-week need

questions.q:
Four classmates do the breath-holding activity twice: first after a normal breath, then after a deep breath. Their times are: Asha 20 s and 32 s; Bina 25 s and 38 s; Chetan 30 s and 45 s; Dev 28 s and 40 s.
(i) Whose time went up the most after the deep breath, and by how many seconds?
(ii) Why does a deep breath help, according to Ajji?
(iii) Why does every one of them have to breathe again in the end?
(iv) The chapter compares going without oxygen with going without food or water. State the comparison.
(v) A fifth student, Esha, writes that she held her breath for 10 minutes. Should the class accept her result? Give a reason.
questions.a: (i) Chetan: 45 - 30 = 15 s (Asha and Dev rose by 12 s, Bina by 13 s). (ii) Taking deep breaths gets more fresh air into the lungs. (iii) The air we breathe has oxygen, which the body needs to perform its functions; when the breath is held, the body does not get enough oxygen. (iv) We can survive without food or water for a few days, but not without oxygen for even a few minutes. (v) No: the best time in the class is 45 s, and we cannot survive without oxygen for even a few minutes, so 10 minutes is a mistake in timing or recording.
s: (i) Chetan, 15 s
(ii) more fresh air reaches the lungs
(iii) the body runs short of oxygen
(iv) a few days without food or water, not even a few minutes without oxygen
(v) rejects 10 minutes, using the class data and the few-minutes fact

questions.q:
At a science fair, four groups each fill a jar with beads to show the parts of air: blue for nitrogen, red for oxygen and white for argon, carbon dioxide and other gases. Their bead counts are:
Group | Blue | Red | White | Total
P | 78 | 21 | 1 | 100
Q | 156 | 42 | 2 | 200
R | 70 | 28 | 2 | 100
S | 150 | 42 | 8 | 200
(a) Which two groups' jars match the composition of air?
(b) In Group S's jar, which colours are wrong, and by how many beads?
(c) What wrong idea about oxygen would a visitor take away from Group R's jar?
(d) Only one jar can go to the district fair. Which would you send, P or Q? Give a judgement that uses the bead counts.
questions.a: (a) P and Q (78:21:1 out of 100, and 156:42:2 out of 200). (b) Blue should be 156, so it is 6 short; white should be 2, so it has 6 too many (red, 42, is right). (c) It shows 28 oxygen in 100, so a visitor would think air has more oxygen than it does (it has 21 in 100). (d) Either with a reason: P is quicker to count and matches the 100-square picture of air directly; Q shows the small share of argon, carbon dioxide and other gases as 2 beads, which is easier to notice, but takes longer to set up.
s: Part (a): P and Q
Part (b): blue 6 short, white 6 extra
Part (c): shows too much oxygen, 28 instead of 21 in 100
Part (d): a choice between P and Q justified with the counts

questions.q:
Rohit writes this paragraph for his class magazine. It has five mistakes. Find each one and write the correct version.
'Air is a single gas called oxygen. Oxygen makes up 78% of the air. Like food, oxygen is something we can go without for a few days. Moving air is called wind only when it blows fast, as in a storm. Windmills are useful, but they can do only one job: generating electricity.'
questions.a: (1) Air is not one gas: it is a mixture of gases (nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and others). (2) 78% is nitrogen; oxygen is 21%. (3) We can go without food or water for a few days, but not without oxygen for even a few minutes. (4) All moving air is wind; it may blow gently as a breeze or fast as a storm. (5) Windmills can also run flour mills and pull up water from wells, as well as generate electricity.
s: Air is a mixture of gases
Nitrogen 78%, oxygen 21%
Few days without food or water, not even a few minutes without oxygen
Breeze and storm are both wind
Windmills also run flour mills and pull up water

questions.q: Four families have no pump and no vehicle, and each needs drinking water today. Which family is most likely to get usable freshwater, and for the right reason?
questions.a: The Patils, as the village pond is part of the small, easily reached share
o: The Patils, as the village pond is part of the small, easily reached share
The Negis, as the glacier above them holds a huge store of freshwater
The Raos, as plenty of freshwater lies deep underground below their own farm
The Fernandes family, as the sea all round their island never dries up

questions.q: A school group visits an old stepwell in Jodhpur. Their guide says it holds water even in a year of poor rain. What feature of the stepwell explains this?
questions.a: Its stone-lined trench walls let in water seeping from nearby lakes and ponds
o: Its stone-lined trench walls let in water seeping from nearby lakes and ponds
Its walls are sealed so tightly that it collects only rain falling into its mouth
It is filled with sea water, which is made fit to drink by passing through the stone blocks
It is fed only by melting snow carried down from the mountains each summer

questions.q:
Read the statements about water on Earth.
Statement 1: Water covers about two-thirds of the Earth's surface, yet most of it cannot be used directly for drinking or farming.
Statement 2: Freshwater stored in ice sheets and underground is the easiest freshwater to reach.
Statement 3: Rainwater harvesting is a new idea, so it is found only in buildings made in recent years.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only

questions.q: In a village in Rajasthan, Kamala walks 3 km each morning to fetch drinking water, while a large house at the end of her lane has its own tap. Which idea from the chapter does this show most directly?
questions.a: Not everyone has the same kind of access to water
o: Not everyone has the same kind of access to water
Most of the water on Earth is saline and salty
Freshwater locked in ice sheets is hard to reach
Water covers about two-thirds of Earth's surface

questions.q: A residential society in Chennai lists four habits for its water-saving week. Which habit does NOT help to conserve water?
questions.a: Washing the car daily with a hose pipe left running
o: Washing the car daily with a hose pipe left running
Fixing the leaking taps in the society's common area
Collecting rainwater from the terraces in a tank
Turning off the tap while soaping hands and utensils

questions.q: A town's lake is full of plastic wrappers, and a small factory empties its waste into it. The town lists four plans. Which plan deals with the cause of the lake's problem rather than finding water elsewhere?
questions.a: Stopping the factory from emptying its waste into the lake
o: Stopping the factory from emptying its waste into the lake
Digging a much deeper well to reach the water lying underground
Building roof tanks to collect rain on every house
Fixing the leaking taps in the town's public buildings

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Water from a lake full of plastic bags and factory waste is not fit to drink.
Reason (R): Freshwater sources are limited, and many parts of India face a shortage of water.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A house has a roof of 40 square metres and gets 750 mm of rain in a season. If 1 mm of rain on 1 square metre gives 1 litre, the most water the roof can harvest that season is ___ litres. (Write digits only, no commas.)

True or False? 'The old stepwells of Rajasthan and Gujarat were built because those regions had water to spare, so a stepwell only had to catch the rain falling into it.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. Stepwells (bawadi in Rajasthan, vav in Gujarat) were built as a response to the scarcity of water in these regions. They store not only rainwater but also water seeping in from nearby lakes, ponds and rivers through their stone-lined trench walls.
s: Verdict: False
Built because water was scarce; they also store water seeping from lakes, ponds and rivers

questions.q:
Aman says, 'The Himalayan glaciers hold huge amounts of freshwater, so nobody in north India should ever be short of water.'
(a) In what form is the freshwater in a glacier?
(b) Use the chapter to explain why this freshwater does not end the shortage.
questions.a: (a) As ice sheets or snow. (b) Freshwater in ice sheets and snow is difficult to access; only a very small fraction of freshwater, in ponds, rivers, lakes and wells, is easily accessible.
s: Part (a): ice sheets or snow
Part (b): ice and snow are difficult to access; only a small fraction in ponds, rivers, lakes and wells is easily accessible

questions.q:
In a family of 4, each person brushes twice a day and leaves the tap running for 2 minutes each time. The tap lets out 6 litres a minute.
(a) How much water does the family use for brushing in a day?
(b) If each person instead uses a mug holding half a litre each time, how much water does the family save each day?
questions.a: (a) 6 x 2 x 2 x 4 = 96 litres a day. (b) With mugs: 0.5 x 2 x 4 = 4 litres; saving = 96 - 4 = 92 litres a day.
s: Part (a): 96 litres a day
Part (b): 4 litres with mugs, saving 92 litres a day

questions.q:
Ritu's family fixes its leaking taps. Her uncle laughs: 'Why bother? Water is renewable; nature gives it back.'
(a) Is water a renewable resource?
(b) Give one reason from the chapter why it must still be saved.
questions.a: (a) Yes, water is a renewable resource. (b) Any one: usable freshwater is limited, since most water is saline and only a small fraction is easily accessible; or many parts of India face a shortage and people walk long distances for drinking water.
s: Part (a): yes, water is renewable
Part (b): usable freshwater is limited, or there are shortages in many places

questions.q:
(a) Water is used for drinking, cooking, washing, growing crops and in industry. For how many of these five uses does the chapter say sea water is fit?
(b) Using (a), explain why a town on the coast can still run short of water.
questions.a: (a) None (0): sea water is saline, and saline water is not fit for domestic, agricultural or industrial use. (b) The sea at its doorstep cannot meet any of these needs, so the town depends on limited freshwater from rivers, lakes, wells or underground, which may not be enough.
s: Part (a): none, because sea water is saline and unfit for these uses
Part (b): the town depends on limited freshwater sources

questions.q: Imran claims, 'A stepwell is just a well with steps. It can hold only the rain that falls straight into it.' Test his claim using the chapter.
questions.a: No. A stepwell stores rainwater and also water seeping from nearby lakes, ponds and rivers. The walls of its trenches are lined with blocks of stone that allow seepage of water, so water keeps coming in even after the rain. Such stepwells (bawadi, vav) were built because water was scarce.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Stepwells also store water seeping from nearby lakes, ponds and rivers
Stone-lined trench walls allow the seepage

questions.q: A family has a roof of 60 square metres and wants to fill a 30,000-litre tank in one rainy season. The season brings 450 mm of rain, and its pipes catch 90% of the rain on the roof. Take 1 mm of rain on 1 square metre as 1 litre. Show that the tank cannot be filled, and find how much rain, to the nearest mm, would be needed to fill it.
questions.a: Rain on the roof: 60 x 450 = 27,000 litres; 90% caught = 24,300 litres, which is 5,700 litres less than 30,000, so the tank cannot be filled. Needed: 30,000 / (60 x 0.9) = 30,000 / 54 = about 556 mm of rain.
s: Water caught: 24,300 litres
Comparison: 5,700 litres short of 30,000
Rain needed: about 556 mm

questions.q: In a water audit, the calculation 5 x 4 x 30 = 600 litres gives the water a family saves in a month. Write the situation: say what the 5, the 4 and the 30 stand for, and name the change in habit that saves the water.
questions.a: E.g. Each of the 4 family members saves 5 litres a day by turning off the shower while soaping, for 30 days in a month: 5 litres per person per day x 4 people x 30 days = 600 litres saved.
s: 5: litres saved per person each day, with a named habit change
4: people in the family
30: days in the month

questions.q:
A school in Pune pipes the rain from its 500 square metre flat roof into a storage tank. Take 1 mm of rain on 1 square metre as 1 litre. Last monsoon brought 700 mm of rain, and the pipes caught 80% of the rain on the roof. The school uses 4,000 litres of water a day.
(a) How many litres did the school collect?
(b) For how many school days would this water last?
(c) A second school in the same town wants to store 4,200 litres a day for 80 days from the same monsoon, with the same 80% catch. What roof area does it need?
(d) A trustee suggests digging a stone-lined pit like a bawadi instead of a sealed tank. Give one advantage and one drawback of this idea for the school, using the chapter, and your judgement.
questions.a: (a) 500 x 700 = 3,50,000 litres fall; 80% = 2,80,000 litres. (b) 2,80,000 / 4,000 = 70 days. (c) 4,200 x 80 = 3,36,000 litres; each square metre gives 700 x 0.8 = 560 litres, so 3,36,000 / 560 = 600 square metres. (d) Advantage: stone-lined walls allow seepage, so a bawadi also gathers water seeping from nearby lakes, ponds and rivers, not just rain. Drawback: on a school ground with no lake, pond or river nearby there is nothing to seep in, so it would gather little more than the tank. Judgement: worth it only if a water body is close by.
s: Part (a): 2,80,000 litres
Part (b): 70 days
Part (c): 600 square metres
Part (d): an advantage (seepage) and a drawback (needs a nearby water body) with a judgement

questions.q:
Students clean a 1 km stretch of river in their town and record what they find: 420 plastic bags, 180 food wrappers, 6 pipes carrying waste from homes and 2 pipes from a small dye factory. The river flows all year, yet the town buys drinking water in tankers.
(a) How many pieces of litter did they find in all, and how many more plastic bags than food wrappers?
(b) Name the two kinds of human activity behind the pipes in the survey.
(c) The river never runs dry. Explain why the town still has a water problem.
(d) The town can afford one step this year: a monthly clean-up drive for the litter, or a rule that stops the 8 pipes from emptying into the river. Which should come first? Justify with the survey.
questions.a: (a) 420 + 180 = 600 pieces; 420 - 180 = 240 more plastic bags. (b) Waste from homes and waste from industries being dumped into the river. (c) The waste and trash pollute the water, and polluted water is not fit for consumption by living beings, so a flowing river can still be unusable. (d) Either, with a reason: the pipes send waste in every day, so stopping them deals with a steady source of pollution; the litter is the largest count, 600 pieces, and a clean-up drive also builds awareness, but it returns unless people stop throwing trash.
s: Part (a): 600 pieces, 240 more bags
Part (b): waste from homes and from industries
Part (c): polluted water is unfit for consumption
Part (d): a justified choice that uses the survey counts

questions.q: Your school has 6 drinking-water taps that each leak 20 litres a day, and the garden is watered with a hose pipe. Propose a five-step plan to use less water in the school. Include: (i) the water lost to the leaks in a month of 22 school days, (ii) a step for the leaks, (iii) a step for the garden, (iv) a step that collects water instead of wasting it, (v) one way the plan helps people and the environment, using the chapter.
questions.a: (i) 6 x 20 x 22 = 2,640 litres lost in a month. (ii) Report and fix the leaking taps. (iii) Water the garden with a can or mug so every drop reaches the plants, instead of a running hose. (iv) Harvest rainwater from the school roof in a tank for later use. (v) Freshwater is limited and many people in India must walk long distances for it; using less keeps more water available for all living beings.
s: Monthly leak loss: 2,640 litres
Step for the leaks: fix them
Step for the garden: watering can or mug instead of a running hose
Collecting step: rainwater harvesting
Benefit linked to limited freshwater and unequal access

questions.q:
The old well in a Rajasthan village has dried up. Meera walks 2.5 km to a lake and 2.5 km back, twice a day, carrying 15 litres on each return trip. Her family needs about 60 litres a day. Plastic wrappers float on parts of the lake.
(i) How many kilometres does Meera walk each day for water?
(ii) How much water does she bring home in a day, and how short is the family?
(iii) Which idea in the chapter about access to water does Meera's day show?
(iv) Why might the lake water not be safe even after she carries it home?
(v) The panchayat can fund only one: rooftop rain tanks for 20 homes, or repairing an old stepwell near the village that once collected seepage from the lake. Which would you choose? Justify.
questions.a: (i) 2.5 x 2 x 2 = 10 km. (ii) 15 x 2 = 30 litres; the family is 60 - 30 = 30 litres short. (iii) Everyone does not have the same kind of access to water; at some places people walk long distances to fetch drinking water. (iv) Trash such as plastic wrappers pollutes the lake, and polluted water is not fit for consumption. (v) Either with a reason: roof tanks put water at each home and end the walk, but fill only in the rains; the stepwell stores rain and seepage, lasts longer and serves the whole village, but families still walk to it and it draws on a lake that is being polluted.
s: (i) 10 km
(ii) 30 litres, 30 litres short
(iii) unequal access, long walks for drinking water
(iv) trash pollutes the lake, so it is unfit
(v) a choice weighing how each stores water and whom it serves

questions.q: A goat spends the whole day eating leaves in the shade of a big tree and never steps into the sunshine. Rohan says, 'This goat gets no energy from the Sun.' Which reply is correct?
questions.a: The leaves it eats were made using sunlight, so its energy is from the Sun
o: The leaves it eats were made using sunlight, so its energy is from the Sun
He is right, since an animal gets the Sun's energy only by standing in it
He is right, since the goat's energy comes from the soil the tree grows in
The cool shade itself gives the goat energy, so the Sun has no part in it

questions.q: In a village in Andhra Pradesh, four jobs are going on at noon. In which job is the Sun's heat being used directly, with no device to convert it?
questions.a: Papads spread on the terrace are drying in the hot sun
o: Papads spread on the terrace are drying in the hot sun
Rice is being cooked at noon on a stove that burns LPG gas
Wheat is being ground at a mill turned by a windmill
Water is being boiled over a fire of dry firewood

questions.q:
Arjun has rice and dal for lunch and then sits in the sunshine reading. Read the statements.
Statement 1: The plants that gave the rice and dal used sunlight to make their food.
Statement 2: The energy Arjun gets from his lunch came, in the end, from the Sun.

questions.q:
Match each use of the Sun's energy in Column I with what it gives in Column II.
Column I | Column II

2. Solar cooker | b. Dried chillies for use when fresh ones are not available
3. Solar water heater | c. Electricity
4. Chillies spread out in the sun | d. Hot water for bathing

True or False? 'In a cloudy week, a house with a solar water heater and a solar panel will run short of hot water, but its panel will give as much electricity as usual, because a panel works differently from a heater.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. The panel does work differently (it produces electricity, while the heater heats water), but both capture the Sun's energy. With little sunlight in a cloudy week, the panel also produces less electricity, just as the heater gives less hot water.
s: Verdict: False
Both capture the Sun's energy, so the panel's electricity also falls when sunlight is low

questions.q:
For breakfast Arjun eats a paratha made of wheat flour, stuffed with paneer made from cow's milk.
(a) Trace the energy in the paneer back to the Sun.
(b) How is the path of energy in the wheat shorter than in the paneer?
questions.a: (a) Sun -> grass (uses sunlight to make food) -> cow eats the grass -> milk -> paneer -> Arjun. (b) Wheat is a plant that made its own food using sunlight, so the energy reaches Arjun directly from the plant, without passing through an animal first.
s: Part (a): Sun to grass to cow to milk and paneer
Part (b): wheat is a plant that used sunlight itself, so no animal is in between

questions.q:
Tanvi keeps a healthy potted plant inside a dark cupboard for two weeks. It turns pale and weak.
(a) Which need of the plant, from the chapter, was not met?
(b) A pet rabbit is fed only on such plants. Use (a) to explain why the rabbit's food is now poorer.
questions.a: (a) Sunlight: plants need sunlight to prepare their food. (b) The plant could not make its food without sunlight, so it has grown weak; the rabbit gets its energy by eating plants, so it now gets less from them. The energy that reaches the rabbit begins with the Sun.
s: Part (a): sunlight, which plants need to make food
Part (b): weaker plant means less energy passed to the rabbit that eats it

questions.q:
(a) In the water cycle, what does the Sun's heat do to water?
(b) Ajji spreads wet clothes and sliced mangoes in the sun. Which part of the water cycle is at work in both, and what is left behind?
questions.a: (a) The Sun's heat makes water evaporate. (b) Evaporation: the water in the clothes and the mango slices evaporates in the Sun's heat, leaving dry clothes and dried mango.
s: Part (a): the Sun's heat causes evaporation
Part (b): evaporation in both, leaving them dry

questions.q:
Bhoomi lists four things: drying clothes, a plant making food, reading on the verandah at noon, a solar water heater.
(a) Sort them into those that mainly use the Sun's heat and those that mainly use its light.
(b) Which one of the four is the start of the food we eat, and why?
questions.a: (a) Heat: drying clothes, the solar water heater. Light: a plant making food, reading on the verandah. (b) The plant making food: plants use sunlight to make food, animals eat plants, and we get food from both plants and animals.
s: Part (a): heat for drying clothes and the water heater; light for the plant and for reading
Part (b): the plant making food, with the plant-to-animal-to-us chain

questions.q: Ishita claims, 'The energy I get from eating an egg comes from the Sun, even though a hen never makes its own food.' Is she right? Check her claim step by step.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. The hen eats grains, which come from plants; those plants used sunlight to make their food. The energy passes from the plants to the hen and its egg, and then to Ishita. The chapter says we get food from both plants and animals, and this cycle is possible because of the Sun.
s: Verdict: the claim is correct
The hen eats grain from plants that made food using sunlight
Energy passes plant to hen to egg to Ishita, so it began with the Sun

questions.q: A family uses solar panels to generate electricity, a gas stove to cook food and a windmill to pump water from a well. Explain what would happen to each of the three if there were no sunlight for a week.
questions.a: Solar panels: they capture the Sun's energy, so with no sunlight they would produce little or no electricity. Gas stove: it burns gas, not sunlight, so cooking would go on. Windmill: it is turned by wind, so it would keep pumping water whenever the wind blows.
s: Solar panels stop producing electricity, with the reason
Gas stove keeps working, because it burns gas
Windmill keeps pumping when the wind blows

questions.q: The answer to a question is: 'From the Sun, through the grass.' Write a question about an everyday animal or food for which this is the correct answer, and explain why the answer is correct.
questions.a: E.g. 'Where does a goat grazing in a field get its energy from?' The goat eats grass; grass needs sunlight to grow and make food, so the goat's energy comes from the Sun through the grass.
s: A question about an animal or food that eats or comes from grass
Grass uses sunlight to make food
Energy passes from grass to the animal, so the Sun is the source

questions.q:
Three children watch a cow grazing in a sunny field.
Anu: 'The cow is standing in the sun, so it is getting energy from the Sun.'
Babu: 'No, it is getting energy from the grass, not from the Sun.'
Cheenu: 'It gets energy from the grass, and the grass needed sunlight to grow, so the energy is from the Sun.'
Judge each child's statement, then say what would happen to the cow's energy supply if the field were shaded from the Sun for many weeks.
questions.a: Anu: wrong; standing in the sun does not mean the cow is getting its energy from the Sun. Babu: partly right; the cow gets energy from the grass, but he misses that the grass needs sunlight. Cheenu: right; grass leaves need sunlight to grow, so the cow gets its energy from the Sun through the grass. Shaded field: the grass could not make food and grow well, so the cow would get less food and less energy.
s: Anu's view rejected: standing in sunlight is not how the cow gets energy
Babu's view: partly right, misses the Sun's part
Cheenu's view: correct, grass uses sunlight
Shaded field: grass grows poorly, the cow gets less energy

questions.q:
The Reddy family in Hyderabad has solar panels on the roof. The panels make 12 units of electricity on a sunny day and 4 units on a cloudy day. The family uses about 60 units a week. Their record for four weeks:
Week | Sunny days | Cloudy days
1 | 4 | 3
2 | 5 | 2
3 | 2 | 5
4 | 1 | 6
(a) In which weeks did the panels make at least 60 units?
(b) How many units short was the family in weeks 3 and 4 together?
(c) Why do the same panels make so much less on cloudy days?
(d) The family can either add panels to make 50% more each day, or keep its connection to the city supply for cloudy weeks. Use the data to judge the choice.
questions.a: (a) Week 1: 4 x 12 + 3 x 4 = 60; week 2: 5 x 12 + 2 x 4 = 68; so weeks 1 and 2. (Week 3: 44; week 4: 36.) (b) (60 - 44) + (60 - 36) = 16 + 24 = 40 units. (c) Panels capture the Sun's energy to produce electricity; when cloud hides the Sun, there is little sunlight to capture. (d) With 50% more, a sunny day gives 18 and a cloudy day 6 units: week 3 becomes 66 (enough) but week 4 only 54, still 6 short. So extra panels cover most weeks but not the cloudiest; keeping the city supply covers every week. Credit either decision that uses these figures.
s: Part (a): weeks 1 and 2
Part (b): 40 units
Part (c): panels need sunlight to capture, and cloud cuts it
Part (d): a judgement using the 66 and 54 units with 50% more panels

questions.q:
A school's eco-club compares two ways of cooking rice for its 30 hostel students. A large box cooker kept in the sun takes 2 hours 30 minutes and needs no fuel. The LPG stove takes 30 minutes and uses gas worth Rs 40 for each lunch it cooks. Lunch is served at 12:30 p.m. and dinner at 7:30 p.m. In this season the Sun sets at 6:00 p.m.
(a) The warden wants to use the box cooker for dinner too. Should she? Give the reason first, with the times.
(b) How much does the LPG for lunch cost in a month of 22 school days?
(c) By what time must the box cooker start for lunch, and how many times as long as the stove does it take?
(d) Should lunch move to the box cooker? Justify, weighing the saving against the weather.
questions.a: (a) No: for dinner at 7:30 p.m. the cooker would have to start by 5:00 p.m., but the Sun sets at 6:00 p.m., so it would get only 1 hour of sunlight against the 2 hours 30 minutes it needs. The box cooker uses the Sun's energy directly and cannot cook without sunlight. (b) 40 x 22 = Rs 880. (c) By 10:00 a.m. (12:30 minus 2 hours 30 minutes); 150 / 30 = 5 times as long. (d) Either with a reason: move, because it saves Rs 880 a month and burns no fuel, if cooking starts by 10:00 a.m.; or keep LPG ready, because on cloudy or rainy days there is too little sunlight and lunch must be on time.
s: Part (a): no; start 5:00 p.m., only 1 hour of sunlight before 6:00 p.m. sunset
Part (b): Rs 880
Part (c): start by 10:00 a.m., 5 times as long
Part (d): a decision weighing the saving against cloudy days

questions.q:
Bhoomi lists five things that happened at Ajji's house on one day. For each, say whether the Sun's energy was used directly as heat or light, converted into electricity, or reached through food.

(ii) converted into electricity
(iii) through food, plant made food using sunlight
(iv) direct use for heating water
(v) through food, grass to goat

questions.q: A government school in Barmer, Rajasthan, gets bright sunshine on most days of the year. Plan five different ways the school could use the Sun's energy. For each, say what device or method is used, whether the Sun's energy is used directly or converted into electricity, and one limitation.
questions.a: Any five sensible ways, e.g. (1) Solar panels on the roof for lights and fans: converted into electricity; little output on cloudy days. (2) A solar cooker for the midday meal: direct; cannot cook after sunset. (3) A solar water heater for the hostel: direct; little hot water on cloudy mornings. s: Way 1 with device, direct or converted, and a limit
Way 2 with device, direct or converted, and a limit
Way 3 with device, direct or converted, and a limit
Way 4 with device, direct or converted, and a limit
Way 5 with device, direct or converted, and a limit

questions.q: Kavya has two vegetable beds. Bed A has plenty of earthworms; Bed B has none, and its soil is hard and lumpy. In which bed must she do more digging, and why?
questions.a: Bed B, as no earthworms are there to turn and loosen the soil

Rain falls only on slopes that have no trees on them

questions.q: A builder in Kerala needs one local rock to cut into blocks for the walls of a house and another to cover the roof of its shed. Which pair matches the uses the chapter gives?

Rainwater, as leaves collect it and store it in the stepwells
Minerals, as decaying leaves slowly turn back into rocks and metals

A builder, a museum guide and a jeweller talk about rocks. Match each item in Column I with its use in Column II.
Column I | Column II

questions.q: True or False? 'Cutting the trees of a forest can make its soil poorer even if none of the soil is washed away.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The leaves that fall from trees decay and enrich the soil with nutrients; with the trees gone, no leaves fall and decay there, so the soil gets fewer nutrients even if it stays in place.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: no fallen leaves decaying, so fewer nutrients reach the soil

questions.q:
In the early 1970s, local women in a part of Uttarakhand set out to stop the trees around their villages from being felled.
(a) What did the women do, in the movement known as Chipko?
(b) Why does saving standing trees matter more than promising to plant new ones later? Use the chapter.
questions.a: (a) They encircled and hugged the trees to protect them from being felled. (b) It takes many years to grow a new forest or restore a lost one; in the meantime the animals lose their food and shelter.
s: Part (a): encircled and hugged the trees to stop them being felled
Part (b): new forests take many years to grow, and animals lose food and shelter meanwhile

questions.q:
(a) From what did early humans make hand axes and arrowheads?
(b) A modern mobile phone is very different from an arrowhead, yet it also depends on rocks. Explain how, using what rocks are made of.
questions.a: (a) From rocks (stone). (b) Rocks are made up of minerals, and a basic mobile phone contains about a dozen minerals such as gold, silver, copper and cobalt, so it too depends on rocks.
s: Part (a): rocks
Part (b): rocks are made of minerals, and a phone contains about a dozen minerals

questions.q: Differentiate between a rock and a mineral, and give one example of how people use each.
questions.a: Rocks are made up of minerals; minerals are what rocks contain. Rock use: slate for roofing, laterite as bricks, or granite, sandstone and marble in buildings. Mineral use: metals such as aluminium, gold, copper and iron are extracted from minerals, or minerals are used in phones and cars.
s: Relation: rocks are made up of minerals
One correct use of a rock and one of a mineral

questions.q: Differentiate between how new soil forms and how a lost forest grows back. For each, say what does the work and how long it takes.
questions.a: Soil: rocks are broken apart by the Sun, water and living organisms; this takes a very long time, thousands of years. Forest: new trees grow from seeds (for example, from the droppings of animals and birds) and take many years to form a forest again.
s: Soil: rocks broken by the Sun, water and living organisms over thousands of years
Forest: new trees grow from seeds over many years

questions.q:
A large forest next to a village is cut down.
(a) Give one way this harms the birds and insects that lived in it.
(b) The chapter says every animal depends on other life forms. Use this to explain why the loss spreads beyond the birds and insects.
questions.a: (a) Forests give wild animals, including birds and insects, food and shelter; these are lost. (b) The diversity of life forms ensures food for every living being; when some animals lose their home, the animals that feed on them, or depend on them in other ways, are also affected.
s: Part (a): loss of food and shelter
Part (b): animals depend on other life forms, so the loss passes on to them

questions.q: Kunal says, 'Rocks are useful to us only for putting up buildings.' Test his claim using the chapter.
questions.a: No. Rocks are used in houses, temples, roads and dams, but that is not all: slate is used for roofing and laterite as bricks; humans have made tools such as hand axes and arrowheads from rocks for thousands of years; and rocks are made up of minerals, from which metals such as aluminium, gold, copper and iron are extracted for cars, airplanes, jewellery and phones.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Use beyond buildings: tools such as hand axes and arrowheads
Use beyond buildings: minerals in rocks give metals for products

questions.q: Show that a forest cut down this year cannot be 'replaced' simply by planting the same number of saplings next year. Give three points from the chapter.
questions.a: (1) It takes many years to grow a new forest or restore a lost one, so saplings are not a forest. (2) A forest is a large area of dense growth of many types of plants, not one kind of young tree; the animals that depended on it lose their food and shelter meanwhile. (3) In the gap, the bare soil is not held by roots and is washed away, and soil takes thousands of years to form.
s: New forests take many years to grow
Animals lose food and shelter in the meantime
Soil is washed away and takes very long to form again

questions.q: The copper wire inside a ceiling fan began its journey in the ground. Trace it back in three links, starting from the rock, and say why the chapter asks us to use such materials responsibly.
questions.a: (1) The rock is made up of minerals. (2) Copper, a metal, is extracted from a mineral. (3) The copper is used to make electrical equipment such as the fan's wire. Rocks take thousands to millions of years to form, so the copper cannot be replaced quickly and must be used responsibly.
s: Rock made of minerals
Copper extracted from a mineral and used in electrical equipment
Rocks take thousands to millions of years to form, so use responsibly

questions.q: Compare rocks and forests as resources under these five heads, giving one point for each: (i) two ways people use each; (ii) how long each takes to form or grow back; (iii) what happens when each is used faster than it is replaced; (iv) one Indian example of people caring for forests, and what the chapter asks us to do about rocks; (v) your conclusion about which needs more careful use, with a reason.
questions.a: (i) Rocks: houses, roads, roofing (slate), bricks (laterite), tools, metals from their minerals. Forests: food and shelter for animals, wood and other products. (ii) Rocks take thousands to millions of years to form; a lost forest takes many years to grow back. (iii) Rocks used up are not replaced in our time; cut forests leave animals without food and shelter, and soil without roots is washed away. (iv) Forests: the Chipko movement, where women hugged trees to stop their felling; rocks: conserve them and use them responsibly. (v) Rocks need more careful use because they take far longer to form (a forest can regrow in years if given time); or both, since forests regrow only if not overcut. Credit either with a reason.
s: (i) two uses of each
(ii) thousands to millions of years versus many years
(iii) effect of overuse for each
(iv) Chipko for forests; conserve and use rocks responsibly
(v) a reasoned conclusion

questions.q:
Bhoomi records four soil samples.
Sample | Colour | Seen with naked eye | Seen with a lens
P, forest floor | dark brown | damp; bits of rotting leaves; an earthworm | tiny insects, fine leaf bits
Q, riverbank | light grey | mostly sand; small pebbles | rounded sand grains
R, beside a garbage heap | blackish | bits of plastic and paper | tiny pieces of garbage
S, ploughed farm | reddish brown | loose lumps; roots | fine particles, small roots
(i) Why are the colours different?
(ii) Which sample shows recycling in nature, and how?
(iii) Which sample needs the most care while handling, and why?
(iv) What does the chapter say soil may hold that even this table could miss?
(v) For a vegetable bed, would you choose soil P or soil S? Give a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (i) Samples from different places may contain different materials. (ii) P: fallen leaves decay and enrich the soil with nutrients, which new plants use. (iii) R: soil that has garbage can carry germs that may be harmful, so hands must be washed thoroughly after touching it. (iv) Many small organisms that cannot be seen with the naked eye. (v) Either with a reason: P has nutrients from decayed leaves and earthworms that loosen the soil; S is already loose, giving air and room for roots to grow.
s: (i) different materials
(ii) P, decaying leaves enrich the soil
(iii) R, garbage may carry germs, wash hands
(iv) small organisms we cannot see with the naked eye
(v) P or S with a chapter reason

questions.q:
The forest department rules that at least 900 hectares of a 1,500-hectare forest in the Western Ghats must still be standing after 10 years. Assume no new forest grows in that time.
(a) How many hectares may be cut in all over the 10 years?
(b) Work backwards: what is the most that may be cut each year, at an even rate?
(c) A timber company asks to cut 90 hectares a year. In which year would the forest drop below 900 hectares?
(d) The department could allow the full amount from (b) or a much smaller amount. Which would you advise? Justify using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 1,500 - 900 = 600 hectares. (b) 600 hectares over 10 years, so at most 60 hectares a year. (c) After 6 years 1,500 - 540 = 960 hectares remain; after 7 years 870, below 900, so in the 7th year. (d) A justified judgement, e.g. a much smaller amount: a lost forest takes many years to restore, animals lose food and shelter, and bare slopes lose soil, so staying just inside the rule is not enough; or the full 60 hectares, if the cut patches are left to regenerate before more is cut.
s: Part (a): 600 hectares
Part (b): 60 hectares a year
Part (c): in the 7th year
Part (d): a judgement using slow regrowth, animals or soil

questions.q:
A school in Bengaluru surveys 120 families about their mobile phones. 60 families buy a new phone every year, 45 every 3 years and 15 every 5 years. Each basic phone contains about a dozen minerals, such as gold, silver, copper and cobalt.
(a) On average, how many new phones do the 120 families buy in a year?
(b) If the 60 yearly buyers moved to one phone every 3 years, how many fewer phones would the families buy each year?
(c) Why does the chapter say that rocks and minerals must be used responsibly?
(d) The eco-club can run one campaign: 'Keep your phone 3 years' or 'Plant a tree for every phone'. Which fits the chapter's idea about minerals better? Justify with your answers.
questions.a: (a) 60 + 45 / 3 + 15 / 5 = 60 + 15 + 3 = 78 phones a year. (b) 60 / 3 = 20, so 20 + 15 + 3 = 38 a year: 78 - 38 = 40 fewer phones a year. (c) Rocks, which are made of minerals, take thousands to millions of years to form, so they cannot be replaced quickly. (d) 'Keep your phone 3 years' fits better: it cuts the use of minerals directly (40 fewer phones a year), whereas planting trees helps forests but does not replace minerals that took millions of years to form. Credit a reasoned case for trees only if it says that minerals are not saved.
s: Part (a): 78 phones
Part (b): 40 fewer phones a year
Part (c): rocks and minerals take thousands to millions of years to form
Part (d): a judgement linking the campaign to saving minerals, with the figures

o: The scooter's petrol and the lamp's kerosene, both from petroleum

questions.q: A district has a coal mine and also gets piped natural gas. Which pairing of each fuel with its main use matches the chapter?

questions.q: During a 'Save Fuel' week, four students describe what they did. Whose action does NOT help to conserve fossil fuels?

Simran cycled the 2 km to and from her school each day
Varun's family took the metro to the market
Asha walked to her friend's house next door

questions.q: Four vehicles wait at a red light: a diesel truck, a petrol scooter, a CNG auto and an electric bus. Which of them releases no smoke while it runs?
questions.a: The electric bus, as electric vehicles release no smoke
o: The electric bus, as electric vehicles release no smoke
The CNG auto, as CNG is a fuel that gives out no smoke
The diesel truck, as long as it was bought this year
The petrol scooter, as its engine burns only a little fuel

questions.q: When Ajji was young, her kitchen fire burnt wood, coal and dung cakes. Today she cooks on LPG. What change in the air of her kitchen does the chapter lead you to expect?
questions.a: Less pollution, as LPG is less polluting than those fuels
o: Less pollution, as LPG is less polluting than those fuels

questions.q: In a survey of 40 vehicles on a street, 18 run on petrol, 10 on diesel, 6 on CNG and 6 are electric. The number of these vehicles that burn a fuel obtained from petroleum is ___. (Write the number only.)
True or False? 'A diesel bus, a petrol scooter and a kerosene lamp fill up with three different liquids, yet all three draw on the same fossil fuel.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Petrol, diesel and kerosene are all obtained from petroleum, one fossil fuel formed from the remains of microorganisms and plants buried deep inside the earth. (CNG would be different: it is natural gas.)

questions.q:
Mr Iyer drives 12 km to his office and 12 km back on each of 22 working days a month. His car runs 15 km on 1 litre of petrol.
(a) How many litres of petrol does he use for office trips in a month?
(b) Give two reasons from the chapter why he should take a public bus instead.
questions.a: (a) 12 x 2 x 22 = 528 km; 528 / 15 = 35.2 litres. (b) Using public transport saves fossil fuels, which are limited and will run out; and burning less petrol means less smoke and carbon dioxide polluting the air.
s: Part (a): 35.2 litres
Part (b): saves limited fossil fuel and reduces air pollution

questions.q:
A family uses a diesel generator, a CNG car, a kerosene lamp and electricity from the city supply.
(a) Which two of the fuels they burn come from petroleum?
(b) Which fossil fuel does the family most probably depend on, without burning any at home, through the city supply? Decide from the main use of each fossil fuel, and explain.
questions.a: (a) Diesel and kerosene (CNG is natural gas). (b) Coal: coal is mainly used for the production of electricity, so the city supply that lights their home probably comes from burning coal at a power station. (Natural gas is also used to generate electricity; accept it with that reason, but coal is the fossil fuel whose main use is electricity.)
s: Part (a): diesel and kerosene
Part (b): coal, because it is mainly used to produce electricity

questions.q:
Back in the city after their holiday, Bhoomi and Surya notice two things: there are very few trees, and the air smells of smoke.
(a) What does Amma say is the cause of the smoke?
(b) What alternative does she point to, and why does it help?
questions.a: (a) Fossil fuels being used in vehicles generate smoke. (b) Electric vehicles, which do not release any smoke, so the air is polluted less.
s: Part (a): fossil fuels burnt in vehicles
Part (b): electric vehicles release no smoke

questions.q:
(a) Why does the chapter say we need to explore alternate sources of energy?
(b) Name one source from earlier in this chapter that makes electricity without burning any fuel, and say what it uses.

s: Part (a): fossil fuels are limited and will run out
Part (b): windmill (wind) or solar panel (Sun)

questions.q: Priya argues, 'Coal is made from plants, and plants grow back every year. So coal will never run out.' Test her argument.
questions.a: No. Coal is formed from the remains of plants and microorganisms buried deep inside the earth, but the change takes millions of years. Coal is found in limited quantities and, once used, it is exhausted, so it is a non-renewable resource that can run out.
s: Verdict: the argument is wrong
Coal takes millions of years to form from buried remains
Limited and exhausted once used, so it can run out

questions.q: A town replaces every coal and wood stove in its homes with LPG. Show that this step cannot, on its own, end the town's air pollution from fossil fuels.
questions.a: LPG (Liquefied Petroleum Gas) is less polluting than coal, wood or dung cakes, but it is still obtained from petroleum, a fossil fuel, and burning fossil fuels produces carbon dioxide. Over-dependence on fossil fuels for transportation also causes large-scale air pollution: vehicles burning petrol and diesel keep giving out smoke, which the kitchen change does not touch. So the town also needs steps such as walking or cycling, public transport or electric vehicles.
s: LPG is less polluting but still a fossil fuel that gives carbon dioxide when burnt
Vehicles burning petrol and diesel still produce smoke
So kitchens alone cannot end it; transport must change too

questions.q:

questions.q: The answer to a question is: 'Coal.' Write a question about lights and fans in a city for which this is the correct answer, and explain why, using the chapter.

questions.q: Explain two ways in which human activities that burn fossil fuels pollute the air, and propose three actions that can reduce this pollution. For each action, say why it helps.
questions.a: Ways: (1) Vehicles burning petrol and diesel release smoke and carbon dioxide; over-dependence on fossil fuels for transport has caused large-scale air pollution. (2) Burning fossil fuels such as coal as domestic fuels also produces smoke and carbon dioxide; over-dependence on fossil fuels as domestic fuels adds to the pollution. Actions: (3) Walk or cycle to nearby places, so no fuel is burnt. (4) Use public transport, so one bus replaces many cars and less fuel is burnt. (5) Use cleaner fuels such as CNG, or electric vehicles that release no smoke.

Domestic burning of fossil fuels such as coal

questions.q:
A town council proposes five steps to save fuel and clean the air. Judge each step as helpful or harmful, giving a reason from the chapter.
(1) Keep bicycles off the main roads so that cars can move faster.
(2) Run more city buses on every route.
(3) Help auto owners to switch from diesel to CNG.
(4) Ask families to cook on coal stoves so that LPG lasts longer.
(5) Hold a 'walk to school' day for children who live within 1 km.
questions.a: (1) Harmful: cycling to nearby places conserves fossil fuels; pushing cyclists into cars burns more fuel. (2) Helpful: using public transport conserves fossil fuels and means less smoke. (3) Helpful: CNG is a cleaner fuel than diesel, though it is still a fossil fuel. (4) Harmful: coal is a more polluting domestic fuel; LPG and natural gas replaced it because they pollute less. (5) Helpful: walking to nearby places burns no fuel.
s: Step 1 harmful, cycling saves fuel
Step 2 helpful, public transport
Step 3 helpful, cleaner fuel but still fossil
Step 4 harmful, coal pollutes more than LPG
Step 5 helpful, walking burns no fuel

questions.q:
In a small town, 45 people each drive their own car 10 km to an industrial area and 10 km back every day. Each car runs 15 km on 1 litre of petrol. A diesel bus doing the same 20 km round trip runs 4 km on 1 litre. At the busiest hour about 180 people need a ride, and every bus seats 50.
(a) How many litres of petrol do the 45 cars use in a day?
(b) Work backwards: at least how many car drivers must switch to one bus before the bus uses less fuel than the cars it replaces?
(c) For the same money the council can buy 4 CNG buses or 2 electric buses. How many of the 180 riders would each choice leave without a seat?
(d) Which buses should the council buy? Justify using (c) and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 45 x 20 / 15 = 60 litres. (b) One car uses 20 / 15 = 1.33 litres a day; the bus uses 20 / 4 = 5 litres; 5 / 1.33 = 3.75, so at least 4 drivers: three cars burn 4 litres, which is less than the bus's 5 litres; four cars burn 5.33 litres, which is more than 5. (c) 4 CNG buses seat 200, so none is left out; 2 electric buses seat 100, so 80 are left without a seat. (d) Either with a reason: CNG buses carry everyone and CNG is cleaner than petrol or diesel, but it is still a fossil fuel; electric buses release no smoke at all, but 80 people may keep driving cars, adding smoke.
s: Part (a): 60 litres
Part (b): at least 4 drivers
Part (c): CNG leaves none, electric leaves 80
Part (d): a decision weighing seats against smoke

questions.q:
A power station burns about 8,000 tonnes of coal every day to supply a district with electricity. The district plans a windmill farm on nearby hills, where the wind is strong in most months but calm for about 120 days a year. On windy days the farm could supply the whole district; on calm days the coal station would have to run.
(a) How much coal does the station burn now in a year of 365 days?
(b) With the windmill farm, how much coal would be burnt in a year, and how much saved?
(c) Why can the windmill farm not replace the coal station completely?
(d) Some members want a second coal station instead, for steady supply. Give your judgement, using your answers and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 8,000 x 365 = 29,20,000 tonnes. (b) 8,000 x 120 = 9,60,000 tonnes burnt; 29,20,000 - 9,60,000 = 19,60,000 tonnes saved. (c) Windmill wings turn only when the wind blows; on the calm days no electricity is made, so the coal station is still needed. (d) A judgement such as: the windmill farm with the old station as backup saves 19,60,000 tonnes of a limited fuel and its smoke; a second coal station gives steady power but uses up more coal, which is limited and will run out, and adds smoke and carbon dioxide. Credit the second station only if the costs are weighed.
s: Part (a): 29,20,000 tonnes
Part (b): 9,60,000 burnt, 19,60,000 saved
Part (c): no wind, no electricity on calm days
Part (d): a judgement weighing steady supply against limited coal and pollution

questions.q: A quiz card lists: coal, air, forest, soil, water, natural gas, rocks and minerals. Using the chapter's classification, the number of renewable resources on the card is ___.

s: Verdict: False
Correction: air is renewable, natural gas is non-renewable because it is limited and takes millions of years to form

questions.q:
(a) Classify coal, natural gas, forests and minerals as renewable or non-renewable.
(b) Which of these four could still be lost to people for a long time even though nature can renew it, and how?
questions.a: (a) Renewable: forests. Non-renewable: coal, natural gas, minerals. (b) Forests: if trees are cut on a large scale, faster than the many years a forest takes to regrow, the forest is lost for a long time.
s: Part (a): forests renewable; coal, natural gas and minerals non-renewable
Part (b): forests, if cut faster than they can regrow

questions.q:
Arjun says soil is renewable, 'because rocks keep breaking down into new soil'. Meena says soil is non-renewable.
(a) Whose classification matches the chapter?
(b) Why is Arjun's reason not enough?
questions.a: (a) Meena's: the chapter lists soil as non-renewable. (b) Soil does form from rocks broken apart by the Sun, water and living organisms, but this takes thousands of years, which is not a reasonable period of time, so soil that is lost is not replenished in time.
s: Part (a): Meena, soil is non-renewable
Part (b): soil forms only over thousands of years, not within a reasonable period

questions.q:
Ritu makes tea: water from the tap, tea leaves and milk, heated on a piped natural gas stove.
(a) Name one renewable and one non-renewable resource she uses.
(b) Which of the two should her family try harder to save, and why?
questions.a: (a) Renewable: water (or the plants that give tea leaves). Non-renewable: natural gas. (b) Natural gas, because it is found in limited quantities, takes millions of years to form and is exhausted once used; water is renewed by nature, though it too must be used judiciously.
s: Part (a): water as renewable, natural gas as non-renewable
Part (b): natural gas, since it is limited and not replenished

questions.q:
In a table of the natural resources used in daily activities, the row 'Making kites' is left blank.
(a) Name a natural resource used to make a paper kite and another used to fly it.
(b) Classify both of them as renewable or non-renewable.
questions.a: (a) Making it: wood or bamboo and paper, which come from forests. Flying it: air, moving as wind. (b) Both forests and air are renewable resources.
s: Part (a): forests (wood, bamboo, paper) to make it, air (wind) to fly it
Part (b): both renewable

questions.q: Deepa claims, 'Renewable resources are restored by nature, so we can use them as freely as we like. Only non-renewable resources need to be saved.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Partly right. Non-renewable resources such as coal and petroleum are limited and must be conserved. But renewable resources must also be used judiciously: forests take many years to regrow and usable freshwater is limited, so overuse can exhaust them for a long time.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: non-renewable resources are limited and must be conserved
Wrong part: renewable resources also need judicious use, with forests or water as the example

questions.q: Manav claims, 'Every human-made resource is made from natural resources.' Check his claim using the chapter and two examples.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. The chapter says we use natural resources to make many useful things, such as electric bulbs, furniture, solar panels and bicycles, and calls these human-made resources. For example, a bicycle is made from metals extracted from minerals in rocks, and a mobile phone contains about a dozen minerals such as gold, copper and cobalt.
s: Verdict: the claim is correct
Human-made things are made using natural resources
Two examples traced to their natural resources

questions.q: Write a list of four things for which this sorting is correct: two renewable natural resources, one non-renewable natural resource and one human-made resource. Give the reason for each.
questions.a: E.g. Water and air: renewable natural resources, renewed by nature within a reasonable period. Coal: non-renewable, takes millions of years to form and is exhausted once used. A bicycle: human-made, created by people from natural resources. (Any correct set with reasons.)

One non-renewable natural resource with a reason
One human-made resource with a reason

questions.q:
Sahil sorts eight resources into a table:
Renewable: air, coal, forests, minerals
Non-renewable: water, soil, natural gas
Human-made: solar panel, wood
Find the four mistakes in his table and correct each one, with a reason.
questions.a: (1) Coal is non-renewable: it takes millions of years to form and is exhausted once used. (2) Minerals are non-renewable: they are not replenished within a reasonable period. (3) Water is renewable: nature renews it. (4) Wood is not human-made: it comes from forests, a natural (renewable) resource. (Air, forests, soil, natural gas and the solar panel are placed correctly.)
s: Coal moved to non-renewable
Minerals moved to non-renewable
Water moved to renewable
Wood is natural, from forests

questions.q: Nikhil reasons, 'Coal is formed from plants, and forests are made of plants. So if forests are renewable, coal must be renewable too.' Evaluate his reasoning in five points.
questions.a: (1) It is true that coal is formed essentially from the remains of plants and microorganisms. (2) But it forms only after they are buried deep inside the earth, and the change takes millions of years. (3) Forests are renewable because new trees grow from seeds within a reasonable period, some years. (4) Coal is found in limited quantities and is exhausted once used; it is not replenished within a reasonable period. (5) So coal is non-renewable and forests are renewable: what matters is the time to replenish, not what the resource came from.
s: Accepts that coal comes from plant remains
Coal takes millions of years to form underground
Forests regrow within a reasonable period
Coal is limited and exhausted once used
Conclusion: classification depends on time to replenish

questions.q:
In one month a school uses 40,000 litres of water, piped natural gas for the canteen, 300 units of electricity from a coal power station and 50 reams of paper. Next month it uses 36,000 litres of water, 240 units of electricity and 44 reams of paper; its natural gas use stays the same.
(i) Name the natural resource behind each of the four, and classify each as renewable or non-renewable.
(ii) How many litres of water, units of electricity and reams of paper are saved?
(iii) Which natural resource does the paper saving help, and why is it worth saving even though that resource is renewable?
(iv) Which of the savings does most for non-renewable resources? Explain.
(v) Suggest the school's next target, with a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (i) Water: renewable. Natural gas: non-renewable. Electricity: coal, non-renewable. Paper: forests, renewable. (ii) 40,000 - 36,000 = 4,000 litres; 300 - 240 = 60 units; 50 - 44 = 6 reams. (iii) Forests: they are renewable, but it takes many years to grow a new forest or restore a lost one, so they need time to regenerate. (iv) The electricity saving: 60 units less means less coal burnt, and coal is limited; natural gas, also non-renewable, was not cut. (v) E.g. cut natural gas use, since it is non-renewable and was the only resource not reduced (any sensible target with a chapter reason).
s: (i) four resources classified correctly
(ii) 4,000 litres, 60 units and 6 reams
(iii) forests, which take many years to regrow
(iv) electricity saving, because coal is non-renewable
(v) a next target with a reason

questions.q:
A Class 6 student lists nine things her family used on Sunday: water from the tap, air through the open window, piped natural gas for cooking, soil in the flower pots, firewood for a bonfire, a wooden table, a bicycle, an electric bulb, and a smooth pebble from the riverbank that she uses as a paperweight.
(a) How many of the nine are human-made resources? Name them.
(b) Of the natural resources, how many are renewable and how many non-renewable?
(c) Which human-made item on the list is made from a renewable resource? Explain.
(d) The family wants to cut down on one resource first: the natural gas or the firewood. Which should it be? Justify using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 3: the wooden table, the bicycle and the electric bulb. (b) Renewable: water, air, firewood (forest) = 3. Non-renewable: natural gas, soil, rock (the river pebble) = 3. (c) The wooden table, made from wood from forests, which are renewable. (d) A justified choice: cut natural gas, because it is non-renewable and will run out; or cut firewood, because burning it gives smoke and forests take many years to regrow, while natural gas is a less polluting fuel.
s: Part (a): 3, the table, bicycle and bulb
Part (b): 3 renewable and 3 non-renewable, correctly named
Part (c): the wooden table, from forests
Part (d): a choice justified with non-renewability or with smoke and slow regrowth

questions.q:
A village forest in the Western Ghats has 200 gooseberry (nellikai) trees. Each tree drops about 30 kg of fruit in a season. By tradition, villagers collect only fallen fruit, and they take half of it, leaving the rest for animals and birds. A trader offers Rs 40 a kilogram for fruit plucked straight from the trees, and wants all of it.
(a) How much fruit falls in a season, and how much do the villagers collect?
(b) Explain how the fruit left behind keeps the forest renewable.
(c) Why would the benefit of any new trees take time to show?
(d) Should the village accept the trader's offer? Justify, weighing the money against the chapter's ideas.
questions.a: (a) 200 x 30 = 6,000 kg fall; the villagers collect half, 3,000 kg. (b) Animals and birds eat it; seeds in their droppings grow into new trees, so the forest is renewed. (c) It takes some years before new trees give fruit. (d) Credit a reasoned decision: accepting all the fruit (6,000 kg) would bring Rs 2,40,000 but leave nothing for animals or new trees, harming the forest's renewal; or a middle path, selling only the 3,000 kg already collected (Rs 1,20,000) while keeping the tradition.
s: Part (a): 6,000 kg fall, 3,000 kg collected
Part (b): animals eat the fruit and seeds in droppings grow new trees
Part (c): new trees take some years to bear fruit
Part (d): a decision weighing income against the forest's renewal
